Now I'm hacking virtual hardware devices for the PDP-7 and controlling them with Forth.

First I made an "Ultimate Machine" device for the PDP-7, inspired by Claud Shannon and Marvin Minsky, whose only purpose is to turn itself off!

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Useless_machine

Bruno Munari called it a "Useless Machine", but Minsky was more compassionate, and appreciated its purpose of turning itself off as being ultimately useful, so he renamed it the Ultimate Machine.

I think there are some deep implications to the halting problem, but I can't quite put my finger on it the way the Ultimate Machine puts its finger on its own off switch.

The Ultimate Machine emulator plugs into the PDP-7 emulator as a virtual device cabinet, which has its own device control IOTs that augment the PDP-7 instruction set.

DEC sold a lot of "plug-in instruction sets in a cabinet" like the Type 340 vector graphics display, its light pen, character generator, subroutine executer, advanced math instructions, etc.

I've never thought having the environment in the version tag (or whatever resembles that) was a good idea. It is a remarkably common thing, though.

But it means that, by definition, we are deploying a different tag to dev, staging, and prod. (Or whatever your pre-prod envs are called.) Hopefully, these all point at the same commit … hopefully¹. (Worse, some schemes out there — not the TFA's — force them to never specify the same commit(!) and we devolve to "let's pray those different commits specify the same tree.)

Just tag a version number. Use the date, if you can't think of a version number. Separately, you maintain some file containing what tag/revision you want on each of your dev/stage/prod/etc. environments. This is basically the same rough scheme as what TFA lays out … but not special. Just text files, in a repo², like everything else. You can do it in a separate repository (I'd recommend) or the same one (I wouldn't recommend, but it can work).

The exemplar question,

> When did we last deploy the www.our-app app to production?

Is just the `git log` of the file that contains the hash that that app should be deployed to.

The SRE in me notes, however, that gitops-based deployments (what all of these schemes are) represent the point in time that a deployment is requested — not when it actually rolls out. Deploys that fail or are blocked on some externality can converge much much later than the git commit instructing them to occur is minted. Also, the SRE in me wants to notes that deploys in any realistic scenario are not a point in time. (It starts when you start bringing up the first replica of your app, and it finishes when the last replica of the older deployment has spun down. Depending on how much bloat you have … it can be a good little span of time.)

(¹TFA's scheme seems to contain a textual reference to the tree sha, but is that checked?)

²If you have worked with Flux or ArgoCD, you're almost certainly doing exactly what I am describing, though those are not the only two such systems capable of it.

As an NLP person it's very hard for me to endorse this explanation, because the Vaswani et al transformer (as it is described here) simply does not work until you add the most important ingredient of all: the positional encoding.

Most of the semantics of a sentence are indicated by the precise order the tokens appear. This is easiest to see in a language like English, since it is visible in two very prominent ways.

First, the morphology is fairly derivational, meaning you can keep adding suffixes to things and English speakers will generally get what you mean. For example, add some more suffixes to that word: derivational-ish-ly. You've probably never heard this specific variant, but you still probably have some idea of what it means anyway. The transformer can only capture these semantics if it has some representation of the fact that the suffixes inflect the meaning of the word's root (presumably something like `deriv`). English encodes this entirely by the position of the suffixes relative to the root. Without the positional information, there is no way to recover it, and sentences would lose much of their meaning, since English depends heavily on this construction.

Second, English has relatively few cases, and thus relies very heavily on the order of words to indicate what is the subject and what is the object. English specifically is Subject-Verb-Object, and the instinct of native English speakers to use SVO ordering is so strong, you will find them inserting nouns and pronouns into sentences that do not actually have subjects at all. "It's raining outside" is the most famous example. This sentence has no subject at all, and yet native English speakers feel a strong need to place "it's" at the beginning.

If the transformer did not have positional encodings it would be completely hopeless to recover what is the subject and what is the object from English sentences. There simply is no other way to reliably tell, other than inspecting the word positions.

It's worth noting we also do have the counterfactual. Generative language models that explicitly exclude positional information, like Latent Dirichlet Allocation, are only able to (essentially) cluster word co-occurrences. That is not as useless as it sounds—if I say "fire house burning ambulence" you kind of get the point even without a subject or an object—but it certainly does not generate the lucid, provoking sentences that modern LLMs do.

But what I want to talk about is trust. The big selling point of crypto has always been that fiat currencies, governments and the banking system can't be trusted. Your money can be seized. You may be subject to capital controls. Also, you're subject to chargebacks and so forth.

So crypto hasn't really eliminated the trust issue. It's just moved it. Instead of governments and the financial system having to be trusted, you're trusting far less accountable hardware vendors who might be completely trustworthy as far as you and they know but they can still be subject to supply chain attacks. An extreme (non-crypto) example of this is the Lebanon pager operation.

I've always maintained the crypto is largely solving non-problems and it treats things in the financial system as bugs when they're in fact features, such as reversible transactions.

Crypto transactions has significant limitations, such as everything needs to be on the blockchain (ie the so-called Oracle Problem), which is the whole reason we have stablecoins, etc.

You can get most of what you want today without a protocol change. mosh only uses ssh for the initial hop, and it just runs whatever ssh is on your PATH, so your ~/.ssh/config applies. Put a ControlMaster/ControlPersist entry in there and only the first tab actually authenticates. Every tab after that reuses the socket, and the "ssh host mosh-server new" step is quick. Each tab still ends up with its own UDP connection, but that's one tiny server process and one key per tab, not a new login.

Sharing one SSP connection across several terminals is a big protocol change, and I'm deliberately keeping mosh-rs wire-compatible with upstream, so I don't want to go off on my own there. For "lots of tabs, one connection" the thing that works well is one mosh session into tmux, and tmux control mode (tmux -CC) if your terminal supports it. That gives you native tabs over a single mosh link, which is about as close to ControlMaster as you can get with mosh's design.

It's interesting, your point makes sense with the caveat of a blurring of terms.

I mean in the sense of, state formation was of such significance that I don't think you can say something like "currency came first" as if currency prior and post state formation is the same thing. It feels like the same sort of "pseudo-currency" with "currency" equivocation.

So if your model is - basic credit in that communal reciprocative sense, then you start trading with more distant outgroups, for this credit doesn't work, so everyone agrees on a currency, someone off in the distance doesn't agree, then states form to adjudicate disputes.

Then it is sensible as a primitive model, but I would just merely suggest that in the same way trying to say currency comes first is kind of a blurring the meaning of currency perhaps to the point of being a stretch, I think in this case to, it will be less orderly. One way this is blurred almost intrinsically in your articulation is via the term dispute resolution process. This could mean anything. It occurs to me that outright conquest and banditry is one way to resolve a dispute. Perhaps in places were there was "spontaneous" centering around a particular currency, this sort of violence was a predicate. I tend to think the need for violence and domination (and mitigations against the same) - what I think of when I think of states "resolving disputes" - was baked into the germ of humanity much earlier than what we might term "state formation". This gets back to the "pseudo-government" point I was trying to make earlier. I think of these things in parallel, rather than in sequence. If at their core humans are violent, such that they make violence, fear violence, and seek tradeoffs to manage violence, then this violence is a driver across currencies and states and trade networks, regardless of a determination of which "came first", if such a determination is even meaningful without greater specificity.

Similarly, I'm not sure if "State formation is a consequence of extended trade networks transacting with currency, currency and trade is not a consequence of state formation" is accurate in the same way. I suppose we have to unblur what "state" means.

Let's compare two scenarios:

1. I live in a village. I buy flour on credit from the miller, because I lack funds and they know I'll be able to pay them back after I sell my own textile goods at market.

2. I travel overseas to a store I've never seen before and I will never see again. I transact $100 on my credit-card purely because my debit card won't work for some reason. I leave with the goods, reminding myself to pay off the balance ASAP with funds I already possess when I get back to the hotel and a laptop.

Technically they both involve "credit", but it's not really equivalent. The first case involves a direct relationship in a community, while the second is indirect, a stranger trusting my card-company. In the first, incurring a debt is an intended feature, in the second the temporary debt is just a weird inconvenient quirk that I'd rather skip entirely because it makes more work for me.

In short, just because someone uses a credit card doesn't necessarily mean it's "credit" in the anthropological sense.
